mainTopic: רב יוסף's objection to רב הונא's ruling like רבי יהודה, and other rulings like רבי יהושע בן קרחה
overview: The amud opens by finishing the dispute between רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה about a dyer who dyed wool differently than the owner asked. רב יוסף turns his face away from רב הונא, who had ruled like רבי יהושע בן קרחה and like רבי יהודה. The גמרא explains why: the ruling like רבי יהושע בן קרחה was needed, but the ruling like רבי יהודה seems obvious. The rule is that a מחלוקת followed by a later סתם משנה is decided like the סתם, and בבא מציעא has a סתם matching רבי יהודה. רב הונא answers that the order of the משנה cannot be trusted between two מסכתות. רב יוסף holds that all of נזיקין is one מסכת, or that the ruling is stated as a fixed הלכה. The גמרא then brings more rulings like רבי יהושע בן קרחה: one may hint to a friend on שבת about working together that evening. And when two equal חכמים disagree, one is strict in Torah law and lenient in rabbinic law. Last, a ברייתא asks whether people who lost their trusted status are accepted back after they repent, and a second version of רבי יהודה's view continues on the next amud.

steps.title: רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה on the dyer who changed the job
steps.stepSummary: רבי מאיר says the dyer pays for the wool. רבי יהודה says the owner pays the dyer, but only the lower amount: either his expenses or the added value.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי מאיר says: the dyer pays the owner the value of his wool. רבי יהודה says: if the added value is more than the expenses, the owner pays the dyer his expenses; if the expenses are more than the added value, the owner pays him the added value.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing its quote of the dispute about a dyer who did not dye the wool the way the owner asked.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי מאיר treats the dyer like a robber who changed what he took, so the dyer keeps the wool and pays its original value. רבי יהודה says the owner keeps the wool and pays the dyer, but the dyer gets whichever amount is lower, because he is the one who went against the instructions.

keyTerms.meaning: The added value. Here, how much more the dyed wool is worth
Expenses, what the dyer spent on the job

steps.whyThisMatters: רב הונא ruled like רבי יהודה here, and that ruling is what רב יוסף questions in the next steps.

phrases.english: Rabbi Meir says:
He gives him the value of his wool.
phrases.notes: The dyer keeps the changed wool and pays the owner what it was worth before, the way a robber who changed what he stole would.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda says:
If the added value is more than the expenses,
he gives him the expenses,
and if the expenses are more than the added value,
he gives him the added value.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי מֵאִיר אוֹמֵר: נוֹתֵן לוֹ דְּמֵי צַמְרוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the quoted source that רב הונא ruled on
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי מאיר: the dyer pays the wool's value. רבי יהודה: the owner pays the dyer the lower of his expenses or the added value.

steps.title: רב יוסף turns away, though the first ruling makes sense
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף shows he is unhappy with רב הונא. The גמרא first agrees that ruling like רבי יהושע בן קרחה was needed, since he was one opinion against many.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף turned his face away. Granted, saying the הלכה follows רבי יהושע בן קרחה was needed. You might have thought that when one חכם disagrees with many, the הלכה follows the many. So he teaches us that here the הלכה follows the one חכם.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף shows he disagrees, and the גמרא is setting up its question by first saying which part of רב הונא's ruling makes sense.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally the הלכה follows the majority, so a ruling like the lone opinion of רבי יהושע בן קרחה adds real information. This sets up the contrast in the next step: the ruling like רבי יהודה seems to add nothing new.

keyTerms.meaning: He turned his face away, a sign he was displeased

phrases.english: Rav Yosef turned his face away.
phrases.notes: He is reacting to רב הונא, who gave both rulings: like רבי יהושע בן קרחה and like רבי יהודה.

phrases.aramaic: בִּשְׁלָמָא הֲלָכָה כְּרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן קׇרְחָה אִיצְטְרִיךְ,
phrases.english: Granted, "the halacha follows Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha" was needed,
since it could enter your mind to say:
when one Sage disagrees with many, the halacha follows the many,
so he teaches us that the halacha follows the one Sage.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Reacts to רב הונא's rulings on the sources quoted
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The objection only shows by gesture here. The verbal part grants that the first ruling was useful, to prepare the real attack.

steps.title: Why say the halacha follows רבי יהודה? It is obvious
steps.stepSummary: The real question: ruling like רבי יהודה is unnecessary, because when a מחלוקת is followed by a סתם משנה, the הלכה follows the סתם.
steps.simpleTranslation: But why do I need "the הלכה follows רבי יהודה"? It is obvious, because when there is a dispute and afterward an unattributed ruling, the הלכה follows the unattributed ruling.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why רב הונא bothered to rule like רבי יהודה, since a known rule already gives that answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is a set rule: if a משנה first records a מחלוקת and a later משנה states one view with no name, the הלכה follows that later unnamed משנה. If that rule already leads to רבי יהודה, רב הונא's statement adds nothing, and that is what bothered רב יוסף.

keyTerms.meaning: A dispute and afterward an unattributed ruling
The halacha follows the unattributed ruling

steps.confusionAlert: "Afterward" means the later of the two משניות in the order they appear. That order is assumed to show which ruling was taught last, and so which one is final. Steps 5-8 argue over whether that order can be trusted here.

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא הֲלָכָה כְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה לְמָה לִי?
phrases.english: But "the halacha follows Rabbi Yehuda" — why do I need it?
It is obvious,
since when there is a dispute and afterward an unattributed ruling,
the halacha follows the unattributed ruling.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא הֲלָכָה כְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה לְמָה לִי? פְּשִׁיטָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns from the part that was granted to the part being attacked
steps.kashyaTarget: רב הונא's ruling like רבי יהודה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The rule מחלוקת ואחר כך סתם already decides the הלכה, so stating it again is unnecessary.

steps.title: The dispute is in בבא קמא, the unattributed ruling in בבא מציעא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא shows the rule fits here: the מחלוקת is in בבא קמא, and a later סתם משנה in בבא מציעא follows רבי יהודה.
steps.simpleTranslation: The dispute is in בבא קמא and the unattributed ruling is in בבא מציעא, as we learned: Whoever changes the agreement is at a disadvantage, and whoever backs out is at a disadvantage.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא proves that this really is a case of a dispute followed later by an unattributed ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: בבא מציעא comes after בבא קמא, so the סתם משנה there counts as coming afterward. That משנה says whoever changes the terms is at a disadvantage, which matches רבי יהודה, whose dyer gets the lower amount. So the הלכה already follows רבי יהודה without רב הונא saying so.

keyTerms.meaning: The one who changes the agreed terms
He is at a disadvantage. He gets the less favorable outcome
The one who backs out of the agreement

steps.whatToRemember: רב יוסף's complaint: ruling like רבי יהושע בן קרחה taught something new, but ruling like רבי יהודה seems already settled by the סתם משנה in בבא מציעא.

phrases.english: The dispute is in Bava Kamma,
and the unattributed ruling is in Bava Metzia,
phrases.notes: בבא מציעא comes right after בבא קמא, so this ruling counts as coming afterward.

phrases.english: as we learned:
Whoever changes the terms is at a disadvantage,

phrases.aramaic: וְכׇל הַחוֹזֵר בּוֹ — יָדוֹ עַל הַתַּחְתּוֹנָה.
phrases.english: and whoever backs out is at a disadvantage.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַחְלוֹקֶת בְּבָבָא קַמָּא, וּסְתָם בְּבָבָא מְצִיעָא, דִּתְנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the question in step 3 by showing the rule really applies here
steps.raayaObject: That this case fits the rule מחלוקת ואחר כך סתם
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה in בבא מציעא: כל המשנה ידו על התחתונה

steps.title: Defending רב הונא: the משנה is not in order
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא needed to rule like רבי יהודה because he holds אין סדר למשנה. Maybe the סתם משנה was really taught first and the מחלוקת came later.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רב הונא, why did he say it? Because there is no fixed order to the משנה. It is possible that the unnamed משנה was taught first, and only afterward came the argument.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why רב הונא still needed to say the הלכה follows רבי יהודה, even though there is a סתם משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule 'מחלוקת then סתם, the הלכה follows the סתם' only works if we know which came later. רב הונא says the order of the משנה is not reliable. So maybe the סתם came first, and then the rule does not settle anything.

keyTerms.meaning: The משנה is not arranged in order of time, so we can't tell which משנה came first
An unnamed משנה, stated without any author's name

phrases.english: And Rav Huna?
phrases.notes: Meaning: why did רב הונא feel he had to say the הלכה follows רבי יהודה?

phrases.english: Because there is no order to the Mishna,
since it is possible to say
the unattributed one was taught first,
and afterward the dispute.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַב הוּנָא? מִשּׁוּם דְּאֵין סֵדֶר לַמִּשְׁנָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב יוסף's question from Steps 3 and 4 on behalf of רב הונא
steps.terutzResolutionType: Undermines the assumption that the סתם משנה came later
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The בבא מציעא סתם came after the בבא קמא מחלוקת, so no ruling is needed
steps.terutzMaskana: The order is not certain, so רב הונא's explicit ruling is needed

steps.title: Then every case should be 'no order'
steps.stepSummary: If the משנה has no order, we could say that about every מחלוקת followed by a סתם, and the whole rule would fall apart.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, in every case of an argument followed by an unnamed משנה, let us say there is no order to the משנה!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רב הונא's answer: it proves too much.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule 'מחלוקת then סתם, the הלכה follows the סתם' is accepted. If אין סדר למשנה applies everywhere, the rule could never be used. So רב הונא's idea seems to cancel an accepted rule.

phrases.english: If so,
every dispute that is followed by an unattributed one,
let us say there is no order to the Mishna!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי הָכִי, כֹּל מַחְלוֹקֶת וְאַחַר כָּךְ סְתָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer given in Step 5
steps.kashyaTarget: רב הונא's use of אין סדר למשנה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the idea applies here, it applies everywhere, and the accepted rule of מחלוקת ואחר כך סתם would never work

steps.title: 'No order' only applies between two מסכתות
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא limits the idea: inside one מסכת the order is reliable, but between two different מסכתות we say אין סדר.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רב הונא? When do we not say 'there is no order'? Within one מסכת. But between two מסכתות, we do say it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives רב הונא's answer: the 'no order' idea is limited to two separate מסכתות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Within one מסכת, the later משנה really is later, so the rule works. Here the מחלוקת is in בבא קמא and the סתם is in בבא מציעא, two מסכתות. So we cannot tell which came first.

phrases.english: And Rav Huna?
phrases.notes: Meaning: how would רב הונא answer this challenge?

phrases.english: When do we not say 'there is no order'?
Within one tractate,
but in two tractates we do say it.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַב הוּנָא? כִּי לָא אָמְרִינַן אֵין סֵדֶר
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limits the scope of the principle
steps.terutzHavaAmina: אין סדר למשנה would apply everywhere
steps.terutzMaskana: It only applies across two different מסכתות

steps.title: רב יוסף: all of נזיקין is one מסכת
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף agrees with the limit, but says בבא קמא and בבא מציעא are really parts of one מסכת, נזיקין. So the order is reliable here.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רב יוסף? All of נזיקין is one מסכת.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why רב יוסף still disagrees: he sees בבא קמא and בבא מציעא as one מסכת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both sides accept that order is reliable inside one מסכת. They only argue whether the three בבות count as one. For רב יוסף they do, so the סתם is surely later and רב הונא's ruling was unneeded.

keyTerms.meaning: The combined מסכת of בבא קמא, בבא מציעא and בבא בתרא

phrases.english: And Rav Yosef?
All of Nezikin is one tractate.
phrases.notes: בבא קמא, בבא מציעא and בבא בתרא are three "gates" of one big מסכת.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַב יוֹסֵף: כּוּלָּהּ נְזִיקִין חֲדָא מַסֶּכְתָּא הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives רב יוסף's side against רב הונא's limit from Step 7
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefines the case so the limit does not apply
steps.terutzHavaAmina: בבא קמא and בבא מציעא are two מסכתות
steps.terutzMaskana: They are one מסכת, so the order holds and the סתם is later
steps.whatToRemember: רב הונא and רב יוסף both agree that order is reliable inside one מסכת. They only argue whether all of נזיקין counts as one מסכת.

steps.title: Another reason: the ruling sits among fixed הלכות
steps.stepSummary: A second reason for רב יוסף: רבי יהודה's view appears in the משנה as a plain, fixed rule, 'whoever changes or backs out loses out,' so it is clearly the final הלכה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or if you want, say: because it is taught together with decided הלכות: Whoever changes the deal is at a disadvantage, and whoever backs out is at a disadvantage.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a different reason why רב יוסף felt רב הונא's ruling was unnecessary.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This reason does not depend on the order of the משניות at all. The משנה in בבא מציעא lists רבי יהודה's ruling as part of a set of plain, decided rules. Being placed among fixed הלכות shows it is the accepted הלכה.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you want, say (introduces another answer)
His hand is on the bottom: he gets the worse deal
One who backs out of an agreement

phrases.english: And if you wish, say:
it is because it is taught
phrases.notes: "It" is רבי יהודה's ruling as it appears in the משנה in בבא מציעא.

phrases.english: alongside decided halachot:
Whoever changes the terms
his hand is on the bottom,
phrases.notes: He ends up with the worse side of the deal.

phrases.english: and whoever backs out
his hand is on the bottom.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי בָּעֵית אֵימָא, מִשּׁוּם דְּקָתָנֵי לַהּ גַּבֵּי הִלְכָתָא פְּסִיקָתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second, independent reason for רב יוסף's view
steps.terutzResolutionType: Alternative proof from the placement of the ruling
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב יוסף's view depends on the order of the משניות
steps.terutzMaskana: Even without order, the ruling is listed among fixed הלכות, so it is clearly the הלכה
steps.whatToRemember: רב יוסף has two reasons: the סתם comes later within one מסכת (נזיקין), or the ruling is listed among fixed הלכות.

steps.title: Hinting to a friend about working together tonight
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא: the תנא קמא forbids saying to a friend 'Does it seem you'll join me this evening?' רבי יהושע בן קרחה permits it.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: A person should not say to his friend, 'Does it seem that you will join me this evening?' רבי יהושע בן קרחה says: A person may say to his friend, 'Does it seem that you will join me this evening?'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another case where רבי יהושע בן קרחה disagrees with others, setting up a ruling in his favor.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question is whether hinting about work for after שבת is a problem. The תנא קמא forbids even a hint. רבי יהושע בן קרחה permits it, since he is not asking outright.

keyTerms.meaning: Does it seem? (a hint, not a direct request)

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
A person may not say to his friend
"Does it seem that you will join me this evening?"
phrases.notes: This is said on שבת. He is hinting that he wants to hire his friend for work once שבת is over.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha says:
A person may say to his friend
"Does it seem that you will join me this evening?"

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: לֹא יֹאמַר אָדָם לַחֲבֵירוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new case connected to רבי יהושע בן קרחה, like the earlier ruling in Step 2
steps.mimraCoreRuling: תנא קמא forbids hinting about joining for work in the evening; רבי יהושע בן קרחה permits it

steps.title: The הלכה follows רבי יהושע בן קרחה
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר בר חנה in the name of רבי יוחנן rules like רבי יהושע בן קרחה: the hint is allowed.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה בר בר חנה said in the name of רבי יוחנן: The הלכה follows רבי יהושע בן קרחה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the final ruling on the ברייתא: we follow רבי יהושע בן קרחה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even though רבי יהושע בן קרחה is one opinion against the תנא קמא, רבי יוחנן rules like him. So saying 'Does it seem you'll join me this evening?' is permitted.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: Rabba bar bar Chana said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan:
The halacha follows Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: הִלְכְתָא כְּרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן קׇרְחָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rules on the מחלוקת from Step 10
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: One may hint to a friend about joining him for work in the evening; the הלכה follows רבי יהושע בן קרחה
steps.whatToRemember: Here too, רבי יהושע בן קרחה is one opinion against another, and an explicit ruling is given to tell us the הלכה follows him.

steps.title: Once a Sage rules strictly, you may not shop for another Sage
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that after a חכם rules something טמא or אסור, the asker may not take the same question to another חכם to get a lenient ruling.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: If someone asked a חכם and he said it is impure, he may not ask another חכם so that he will say it is pure. If a חכם forbade it, he may not ask another חכם so that he will permit it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא. It says you cannot go looking for a second, more lenient opinion after a חכם has already ruled strictly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first חכם's strict ruling stays binding on this question. The ברייתא gives two parallel examples: טומאה (pure or impure) and איסור (forbidden or permitted).

keyTerms.meaning: One who asks a Sage a question

steps.whyThisMatters: This is a basic rule in how people ask halachic questions: once a strict ruling is given, you cannot simply hunt for a lenient answer.

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
One who asks a Sage, and he rules it impure
may not ask a Sage so that he will rule it pure;
phrases.notes: He means a second, different חכם about the very same question.

phrases.english: if he asked a Sage and he forbade it
he may not ask a Sage so that he will permit it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new ברייתא about asking חכמים, brought right after the previous ruling like רבי יהושע בן קרחה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: After a strict ruling by one חכם, you may not ask another חכם to get a lenient ruling.

steps.title: When two Sages disagree: follow the greater one, otherwise be strict
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues. If two חכמים give opposite rulings, follow the one who is greater in wisdom and in number. If neither is greater, follow the stricter one.
steps.simpleTranslation: If there were two חכמים, one saying impure and one saying pure, or one forbidding and one permitting: if one of them is greater than the other in wisdom and in number, follow him. If not, follow the one who is strict.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא now covers a different case: two חכמים disagree with each other at the same time. It tells the asker whose ruling to follow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: First choice: follow the greater חכם. If they are equal, the fallback is to be strict. This is the view of the תנא קמא, which רבי יהושע בן קרחה will now limit.

keyTerms.meaning: Follow the one who rules strictly

phrases.english: If there were two Sages,
one rules it impure and one rules it pure,
or one forbids and one permits,

phrases.aramaic: אִם הָיָה אֶחָד מֵהֶם גָּדוֹל מֵחֲבֵירוֹ
phrases.english: if one of them was greater than the other
in wisdom and in number,
phrases.notes: "In number" is about how many stand with him, so he has more backing than the other חכם.

phrases.english: follow him;
and if not, follow the one who is strict.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָיוּ שְׁנַיִם, אֶחָד מְטַמֵּא וְאֶחָד מְטַהֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same ברייתא with a new case: two חכמים disagreeing at once.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Follow the greater חכם. If neither is greater, follow the stricter view.

steps.title: רבי יהושע בן קרחה: strict in Torah law, lenient in rabbinic law
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע בן קרחה says that when the two חכמים are equal, the answer depends on the type of law. In a Torah law be strict; in a rabbinic law be lenient.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהושע בן קרחה says: In a Torah law, follow the strict one. In a rabbinic law, follow the lenient one.
steps.whatsHappening: A second opinion in the same ברייתא disagrees with the 'always be strict' fallback. It splits the rule by the type of law.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תנא קמא said: if the חכמים are equal, always be strict. רבי יהושע בן קרחה keeps that only for דאורייתא. For דרבנן he says follow the lenient view.

keyTerms.meaning: In a matter of Torah law
In a matter of rabbinic law

steps.confusionAlert: This is the same רבי יהושע בן קרחה as in the previous steps, but here it is a new topic: disagreeing חכמים, not hinting to a friend.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha says:
in a Torah law, follow the one who is strict;
in a rabbinic law, follow the one who is lenient.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן קׇרְחָה אוֹמֵר: בְּשֶׁל תּוֹרָה הַלֵּךְ אַחַר הַמַּחְמִיר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with the תנא קמא's fallback rule by dividing between Torah law and rabbinic law.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Be strict in a disagreement over a Torah law, and lenient in a disagreement over a rabbinic law.

steps.title: רב יוסף rules like רבי יהושע בן קרחה
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף rules that the הלכה follows רבי יהושע בן קרחה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף said: The הלכה follows רבי יהושע בן קרחה.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף gives the final ruling in the argument over two disagreeing חכמים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The practical rule is: when equal חכמים disagree, be strict in a Torah law and lenient in a rabbinic law. This closes the ברייתא about asking חכמים.
steps.whatToRemember: Once a חכם rules strictly, you may not shop around for a lenient answer. When two חכמים disagree, follow the greater one. If they are equal, the הלכה follows רבי יהושע בן קרחה: be strict in a Torah law and lenient in a rabbinic law.

phrases.english: Rav Yosef said:
The halakha follows Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יוֹסֵף: הִלְכְתָא כְּרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן קׇרְחָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Decides between the תנא קמא and רבי יהושע בן קרחה.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The הלכה follows רבי יהושע בן קרחה: strict in Torah law, lenient in rabbinic law.

steps.title: רבי מאיר: people who lost their trust are never accepted back
steps.stepSummary: A new ברייתא: even if these people repent, רבי מאיר says they are never accepted back.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: All of them who repented are never accepted back. These are the words of רבי מאיר.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another ברייתא, about people who lost their trusted status because of their sins. רבי מאיר says that even after they repent, they are never accepted again.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question is whether repentance brings back trust. רבי מאיר's answer is no: the loss of trust is permanent.

keyTerms.meaning: Who went back on their ways (repented)

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
And all of them who retracted,
phrases.notes: "All of them" means people who lost their trusted status because of their sins; the גמרא assumes we know who they are.

phrases.english: are never accepted back;
these are the words of Rabbi Meir.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new ברייתא on a new topic: accepting people back after they repent.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Those who lost their trust are never accepted back, even after repentance.

steps.title: רבי יהודה: private repentance is not accepted, public repentance is
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה says it depends how they repented. If they repented secretly, they are not accepted. If they repented publicly, they are accepted.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה says: If they repented in private, they are not accepted. If they repented in public, they are accepted.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהודה disagrees with רבי מאיר. He says repentance can bring people back, but only if it is done openly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי מאיר said 'never.' רבי יהודה adds a condition: public repentance works, and private repentance does not.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda says:
if they retracted in private,
they are not accepted;
if in public, they are accepted.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר: חָזְרוּ בָּהֶן בְּמַטְמוֹנִיּוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with רבי מאיר by making acceptance depend on how they repented.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Public repentance is accepted. Private repentance is not.

steps.title: Another version: if they sinned in private, they are accepted
steps.stepSummary: An איכא דאמרי gives a different version of רבי יהודה's view. It is based on how they sinned: if they sinned privately, they are accepted after repenting.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say a different version: If they did their deeds in private, they are accepted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a second version of רבי יהודה's opinion. Here the focus is on how they sinned, not how they repented. This version continues past this point.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first version, the key question was how they repented: in private or in public. In this version, the key question is how they sinned. If the sins were done in private, they are accepted back after repenting.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix the two versions. The first version asks how they repented. This version asks how they sinned.

phrases.english: There are those who say:
if they did their deeds in private,
phrases.notes: "Their deeds" means the sins they did, not their repentance.

phrases.english: they are accepted,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a different version of רבי יהודה's view, based on how they sinned rather than how they repented.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If their sins were done in private, they are accepted back after repenting (the version continues beyond this point).
